cards.title: Why Experiment Tracking Exists
cards.teaser: Without experiment tracking, machine learning is a black hole: you train a model, get a number, and have no reliable way to reproduce it, explain how it compares to yesterday's run, or know which code produced it. Tracking converts ephemeral experiments into a permanent, queryable record.

runs.text: Software engineering has version control. ML experimentation, left to its own devices, has a folder named
final_model_v3_REAL_use_this_one.pkl
. The gap is not laziness — it is that ML adds two dimensions that git was never designed to track:
hyperparameter configurations
and
numeric outputs that evolve during training
The problems that experiment tracking solves:

items.text: A model that cannot be re-trained to the same performance level is not deployable with confidence. Tracking captures everything needed to reproduce a run.
Did increasing the learning rate help? Was last week's model better on precision even if this week's is better on recall? Answering these questions requires structured records of every run.

Regulated industries (finance, healthcare) require model documentation that explains which data, code, and parameters produced a deployed model. Experiment tracking is the primary source for that documentation.
Without shared tracking infrastructure, teammates cannot build on each other's experiments — they only share notebooks and hope the environment matches.

runs.text: The 2021 Reproducibility Crisis in ML paper (Pineau et al.) found that fewer than 15% of published results could be reproduced from the information provided. Experiment tracking is the infrastructure that closes this gap in production settings.
Experiment tracking is the system that records every training run so you can reproduce it, compare it to other runs, and explain what produced any given deployed model.

cards.title: The Run Concept
cards.teaser: A run is the atomic unit of experiment tracking — one complete execution of a training script, from loading data to producing an output. Every run gets a unique ID, a timestamp, and a complete snapshot of its inputs and outputs.

runs.text: A
run

represents a single, bounded execution of a training pipeline. When you start a run, the tracking system allocates a unique identifier and begins recording. When the run ends — whether successfully or with an error — the record is sealed.
What a run captures:

items.text: : a unique run ID (e.g., UUID or a human-readable slug), a start time, an end time, a status (running, completed, failed, killed).
: the experiment it belongs to (a named grouping of related runs), the user who started it, and the environment (host machine, Python version, GPU type).
: hyperparameters (all of them — see card 3), the data version, and the code version.
: metrics (loss curves, final accuracy, F1), artifacts (model file, checkpoints, plots), and any tagged notes.

runs.text: Runs are typically organized into
experiments
— named containers that group runs exploring the same hypothesis ("learning rate sweep for BERT-base", "ResNet-50 baseline"). An experiment is the folder; a run is the file.
In MLflow, a run is created with
mlflow.start_run()
and closed with
mlflow.end_run()
. Using it as a context manager (
with mlflow.start_run():
) ensures the run is always closed, even on exception.

A run is one execution of your training code, captured as a permanent record with a unique ID. Everything that went in (parameters, data version, code) and everything that came out (metrics, model files) is attached to that ID.

cards.title: Hyperparameters
cards.teaser: Hyperparameters are the values you set before training begins — learning rate, batch size, number of layers, dropout rate, optimizer type. They are not learned from data; they are the knobs you turn. Tracking them is mandatory for experiment comparison.

runs.text: The term
hyperparameter
distinguishes values that configure the learning process from the model's own learned
parameters
(weights). Hyperparameters are human-chosen; parameters are gradient-computed.
Common hyperparameter categories:

items.text: : learning rate, weight decay, momentum, optimizer (Adam vs SGD vs RMSProp), learning rate schedule.
: number of layers, hidden dimension size, attention heads, dropout probability, activation function.
: batch size, number of epochs, early stopping patience, gradient clipping threshold.
: augmentation strategy, normalization parameters, sequence length, train/validation split ratio.

runs.text: The tracking discipline: log
all

hyperparameters at run start, not just the ones you are sweeping. The ones you think are constant today are often the ones that matter when a colleague re-runs your experiment in a different environment.

Logging only the hyperparameters you varied is the most common experiment tracking mistake. The "fixed" values (optimizer, batch size, sequence length) are equally part of the run's identity — a run logged without them cannot be reproduced.

Hyperparameters are the settings you configure before training — learning rate, batch size, architecture choices. Unlike model weights, they are not learned; they are chosen. Every one of them should be logged at the start of each run.

cards.title: Metrics
cards.teaser: Metrics are the quantitative outputs of training — loss, accuracy, F1, AUC, BLEU, perplexity. Unlike hyperparameters, metrics are logged continuously during training, producing time-series curves that reveal not just how well the model trained, but whether it trained stably.

runs.text: A metric is any scalar value that measures model behavior. Experiment tracking platforms store metrics as
time series
— a sequence of (step, value) pairs where step is typically a training iteration or epoch. The curve tells a story that a final number cannot.
Important metric patterns to track:

items.text: : the gap between them reveals overfitting. A training loss that keeps falling while validation loss rises is the clearest signal that regularization or data is insufficient.
: accuracy, F1, precision/recall, AUC-ROC evaluated on the held-out validation set every N steps. These track whether optimization translates into task improvement.
: unusually large or near-zero gradient norms indicate exploding or vanishing gradients — training instability that final metrics may not surface.
: GPU utilization, memory usage, throughput (samples/sec). A model that trains to the same accuracy in half the time is better for production.

runs.text: In MLflow:
mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", loss, step=epoch)
. The
step
parameter is what creates the time series — omitting it makes all log calls appear at step 0, collapsing the curve to a single point.

Metrics are the numbers that measure how well training is going — loss, accuracy, F1. They are logged as time series so you can see the curve, not just the final value. The curve tells you whether training was stable and when the model stopped improving.

cards.title: Artifacts
cards.teaser: An artifact is any file produced by a run — the trained model, a checkpoint, a confusion matrix plot, a tokenizer vocabulary, a requirements file. Artifacts are what you actually deploy or inspect. Tracking them ties the file to the run that produced it.

runs.text: While hyperparameters and metrics are scalar values,
artifacts
are binary or structured files. They are the tangible output of a run that other systems consume.

items.text: : intermediate model states saved during training. Allow resuming a long training run without starting over.
: confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP plots, sample predictions. Visual evidence of model behavior that metrics alone cannot convey.
: fitted scalers, tokenizer vocabularies, feature encoders. These must travel with the model — inference will break if preprocessing differs from training.
, or a Dockerfile. Without these, the model file is unrunnable.

runs.text: In MLflow:
mlflow.log_artifact("outputs/confusion_matrix.png")
logs a single file;
mlflow.log_artifacts("outputs/")
logs a directory. MLflow also provides framework-specific model logging:
mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, "model")
which captures both the weights and the loading code.

An artifact stored outside the tracking system — for example, just saved to a local path — is not truly tracked. It has no run association, no lineage, and no guarantee it will be findable when the model is promoted to production.

Artifacts are the files a run produces — model weights, plots, environment snapshots. Logging them to the tracking system ties each file to the exact run that created it, so you always know where a model file came from.

cards.title: Code Version Pinning
cards.teaser: Every run must record the exact git commit that produced it. Without the commit hash, two runs with identical hyperparameters may produce different results because the training code changed between them — and you will have no way to know.

runs.text: Code is as much a part of a run's identity as its hyperparameters. A learning rate of
in commit
a3f9b12
may produce a model with 0.87 accuracy. The same learning rate in commit
c8d2e45
— where someone refactored the data loader — may produce 0.83. Without the commit hash, you cannot explain the difference.
What code version pinning requires:

items.text: : the full SHA of the commit at run time, not a branch name. Branches move; commits do not.
: if the repository has uncommitted changes at run time, the commit hash is misleading. Tracking systems should warn — or refuse to run — if the tree is dirty. MLflow Projects enforces this.
: the remote origin, so a colleague can clone and check out the exact commit even if the local repository is gone.

runs.text: MLflow captures the git commit automatically when
mlflow.start_run()
is called inside a git repository. The run detail page shows the commit hash, the branch, and whether the working tree was clean. W&B and Neptune perform the same capture.

Running experiments from a dirty working tree is one of the most common sources of silent irreproducibility. The commit hash is logged, but the actual code that ran included uncommitted changes that the hash does not describe. Enforce clean-tree runs in shared experimentation environments.

Code version pinning means recording the exact git commit hash that was running when the experiment started. Without it, two runs with the same hyperparameters can produce different results and you have no way to explain why.

cards.title: MLflow — The Open-Source Standard
cards.teaser: MLflow is the de facto open-source experiment tracking platform. It provides four components: Tracking (run logging), Projects (reproducible packaging), Models (flavor-agnostic model format), and Registry (model lifecycle management). It runs locally, self-hosted, or on Databricks.

runs.text: MLflow was open-sourced by Databricks in 2018 and has become the most widely deployed self-hosted experiment tracking system. Its four-component architecture covers the full ML lifecycle:

items.text: : the core logging API. Log parameters, metrics, artifacts, and tags. Backed by a SQL store (SQLite locally, PostgreSQL in production) and an artifact store (local filesystem, S3, GCS, Azure Blob).
: a convention for packaging ML code as reproducible units. An
file defines the entry point, parameters, and conda/Docker environment. Run any project with
: a standard model packaging format with "flavors" (PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, ONNX, custom Python). A model logged in the Models format can be served via REST API with
: a versioned catalog of registered models. Models move through stages: Staging, Production, Archived. Provides the lineage link from a run to a deployed model version.

runs.text: A minimal MLflow training script:

explanation.code:
import mlflow
import mlflow.sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Set the experiment (creates it if it does not exist)
mlflow.set_experiment("fraud-detection-v2")

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="rf-depth-sweep"):
    # Log all hyperparameters at the start
    params = {"n_estimators": 200, "max_depth": 8, "min_samples_split": 4}
    mlflow.log_params(params)

    # Train
    model = RandomForestClassifier(**params, random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Log metrics at evaluation time
    acc = accuracy_score(y_val, model.predict(X_val))
    mlflow.log_metric("val_accuracy", acc)

    # Log the model artifact (captures flavor + environment)
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, artifact_path="model")

    # Log any additional artifacts
    mlflow.log_artifact("outputs/feature_importance.png")

runs.text: MLflow autolog (mlflow.autolog()) hooks into popular frameworks (scikit-learn, PyTorch Lightning, XGBoost, Keras) and logs hyperparameters, metrics, and models automatically without explicit log calls. Useful for quick experiments; explicit logging is better for production pipelines where you control what is recorded.

MLflow is an open-source toolkit with four parts: Tracking logs runs, Projects packages code for reproducibility, Models gives models a standard format, and Registry manages model versions through Staging and Production. It is the most common choice for teams hosting their own tracking system.

cards.title: Weights & Biases (W&B)
cards.teaser: Weights & Biases is a commercial experiment tracking platform focused on rich visualization and team collaboration. Its Sweeps feature automates hyperparameter search, and its Reports feature turns experiment results into shareable, interactive documents.

runs.text: W&B (launched 2018 by Lukas Biewald and team) is the dominant commercial offering in the experiment tracking space, particularly popular in research and deep learning teams. Its core differentiators over self-hosted MLflow:

items.text: : interactive metric charts with zoom, smoothing, and run overlay. System metrics (GPU utilization, memory) tracked automatically alongside model metrics. Media logging — images, audio, video, 3D point clouds — is first-class.

: distributed hyperparameter search with grid, random, and Bayesian strategies. A sweep is defined in a YAML config; W&B agents on any machine pick up and run sweep trials, logging results centrally. Early stopping (Hyperband) is built in.

: a Notion-like interface for embedding live charts, run comparisons, and written analysis into shareable documents. Used by teams to communicate experiment results to stakeholders without exporting screenshots.
: W&B Artifacts provides versioned, lineage-tracked storage for datasets, models, and other files. Artifact lineage graphs show which dataset produced which model, which job consumed it.
: native integrations with PyTorch, Keras, HuggingFace Transformers, LightGBM, XGBoost, fast.ai, and many more. Typically one-line:

runs.text: W&B runs a SaaS backend by default (data leaves your environment). A W&B Server self-hosted option exists for enterprise deployments with data residency requirements.

W&B is a commercial tracking platform known for beautiful charts, automatic hyperparameter sweeps, and collaborative Reports that let teams share experiment results as living documents rather than static screenshots.

cards.title: Neptune.ai
cards.teaser: Neptune is a commercial experiment metadata store optimized for large-scale tracking. Its key differentiator is flexible metadata namespacing — any structure of logged data — combined with fast querying across thousands of runs.

runs.text: Neptune positions itself as an
experiment metadata store
rather than an experiment tracker — a distinction that reflects its architectural focus on querying and organizing large volumes of runs across many projects and teams.

items.text: : Neptune logs values into a namespace hierarchy (
). Any depth of nesting, any custom structure. This makes it easy to organize complex logging from multi-stage pipelines.

: the Neptune web UI supports filtering and sorting runs by any logged value. SQL-like queries can be executed programmatically via the Neptune client to retrieve run data into pandas DataFrames for custom analysis.
: Neptune is designed for teams running thousands of experiments — large NLP/CV research labs, AutoML pipelines. Its backend is optimized for high-volume metadata ingestion and fast retrieval.
: Neptune includes a model registry with version management and approval workflows, similar to MLflow's Registry but with tighter integration to experiment metadata.

runs.text: Neptune is SaaS-first. An on-premises deployment option exists for enterprise. Integration is via the
neptune
Python client:
run = neptune.init_run(project="org/project")
followed by flexible key-based logging.

Neptune is a commercial tracking tool built around the idea that metadata is flexible and queryable — you can log anything in any structure and then filter across thousands of runs to find what you need.

cards.title: Comet ML
cards.teaser: Comet ML combines experiment tracking with production monitoring in one platform — it follows a model from training run through deployment, letting teams compare live production metrics against the validation metrics logged when the model was trained.

runs.text: Comet (founded 2017) was one of the first commercial experiment tracking platforms. Its differentiating focus is the
full lifecycle
— connecting training-time experiments to production-time monitoring so teams can detect model drift by comparing live predictions against the training distribution.

items.text: : standard run logging with parameter, metric, artifact capture. Comet's code panel captures the full source code of the training script — not just the git hash — which is particularly useful in notebook-heavy workflows.

: Comet MPM (Model Production Monitoring) logs predictions from deployed models and monitors for distribution shift, data quality degradation, and prediction drift. Alerts trigger when production metrics deviate from training baselines.
: versioned registry that links deployed model versions back to the training experiments that produced them.
: a UI customization system that lets teams build dashboards comparing training and production data side by side.

runs.text: Comet is SaaS with an on-premises enterprise option. Integration:
from comet_ml import Experiment
experiment = Experiment(project_name="my-project")
followed by
experiment.log_parameters()
and
experiment.log_metric()

Comet ML is a commercial platform that tracks experiments during training and then continues tracking the same model once it is deployed — so you can catch when production predictions start drifting away from what you saw in training.

cards.title: Platform Comparison: MLflow vs W&B vs Neptune vs Comet
cards.teaser: The four major experiment tracking platforms share a common core but differ significantly in hosting model, visualization depth, hyperparameter search, and production monitoring scope. Choosing between them is primarily a decision about team size, data residency, and budget.

runs.text: All four platforms log runs, capture hyperparameters and metrics, store artifacts, and provide a comparison UI. The differences matter most at scale and at the boundaries of the ML lifecycle.
Key decision heuristics:

items.text: Regulated industries with data residency requirements
: MLflow self-hosted or W&B Server. Data never leaves your VPC.
: W&B Sweeps is the most integrated and easiest-to-configure distributed hyperparameter search.
: Neptune's querying capabilities and flexible metadata namespacing scale better than MLflow's flat parameter structure.
: Comet is the only platform that natively connects training experiments to production drift monitoring in one UI.

runs.text: MLflow is open source and self-hosted; W&B is commercial with the best visualization and sweeps; Neptune is commercial with the most flexible querying; Comet is commercial with built-in production monitoring. All four do the core tracking job — the differences show up at the edges.

cards.title: The Minimum Reproducibility Set
cards.teaser: Reproducibility is not binary. There is a minimum set of four things you must capture to have any chance of re-running an experiment and getting the same result: hyperparameters, code version, data version, and environment. Missing any one of them makes the run unreproducible regardless of how the other three are tracked.

runs.text: The
minimum reproducibility set
is the smallest collection of artifacts and metadata that, together, allow any ML run to be exactly reproduced. It has four components:

items.text: : the complete set — not just the ones that were varied. Every configuration value that could have been different must be recorded.
: git commit SHA of the training repository. If notebooks were used, the notebook state must be versioned too (nbconvert + git, or a tool like DVC).
: a pointer to the exact dataset used. A file hash, a DVC-tracked version, a dated S3 path, or a Feature Store version number. "The training CSV from the shared drive" is not a data version.
: the complete dependency specification. Options in increasing rigor:
(pins both Python packages and system-level dependencies).
: a specific image SHA that freezes the entire execution environment, including CUDA version and system libraries (strongest guarantee).

runs.text: Why each one is load-bearing:

items.text: : the logic may have changed; same config, different behavior.
: the training distribution may have changed; different data, different model.
: library updates (PyTorch minor versions, numpy) can change numerical precision and convergence behavior.

runs.text: To reproduce any ML run you need exactly four things: the hyperparameters, the exact code commit, the exact data version, and the dependency environment. If any one is missing, the run cannot be reproduced — even if the other three are perfectly recorded.

cards.title: Lineage — From Run to Deployed Model
cards.teaser: Lineage is the chain of provenance connecting a deployed model back through every artifact, run, and dataset that produced it. Without lineage, you cannot answer the question every production ML system eventually faces: 'Exactly what data and code is this prediction based on?'

runs.text: In data engineering,
data lineage
tracks how a data asset was produced from upstream sources. ML lineage extends this concept through the training and deployment pipeline:
A complete lineage chain looks like:

items.text: (run ID: rf-sweep-042, hyperparams logged, produced model.pkl)

runs.text: Each arrow must be a traceable, stored link — not a convention that people try to follow. MLflow's Model Registry stores the
source run ID
on every registered model version, creating the run → artifact → registered model link automatically. The dataset → run link requires explicit logging (
mlflow.log_param("dataset_version", "v2.3.1")
or a dataset artifact logged via
mlflow.log_input()
in MLflow 2.4+).

W&B Artifacts provides a visual lineage graph showing the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of artifact dependencies across runs — particularly useful when model training involves multiple upstream processing steps.

Lineage is not only a compliance requirement — it enables fast incident response. When a model behaves unexpectedly in production, lineage lets you immediately identify the training run, inspect its metrics and hyperparameters, check the data version for anomalies, and determine whether the problem started with data, code, or training configuration.

Lineage is the traceable chain: this dataset produced this feature set, which was used in this training run, which produced this model file, which was registered as this model version, which was deployed as this endpoint. Every link must be a stored pointer, not a convention.

cards.title: Experiment Organization Patterns
cards.teaser: A tracking system full of runs named 'run_1', 'run_final', and 'test_new' is not a tracking system — it is noise with a UI. Naming conventions, tagging schemas, and experiment hierarchies are as important as the tracking infrastructure itself.

runs.text: Experiment tracking platforms store whatever you give them. The discipline of
organization
— deciding what naming conventions, tagging strategies, and experiment hierarchies to adopt — determines whether the tracking system is queryable weeks later.
Recommended organization patterns:

items.text: : one experiment per distinct modeling hypothesis or feature change. "lr-schedule-comparison", "bert-base-vs-distilbert", "augmentation-ablation". Do not put all runs in a single default experiment.
. Encodes the most important dimensions in the name so the table view is scannable without opening each run.
let you filter across experiments. Use a consistent tag schema — ad hoc tags become unsearchable.
). Use a parent run to represent a sweep or a multi-fold cross-validation job; child runs represent individual trials. The parent aggregates the best result.

runs.text: The most expensive experiment tracking failure is not losing run data — it is having the data but being unable to find the right run when you need it. Organization conventions must be established before the first model ships, not retrofitted after hundreds of runs have accumulated.

A tracking system with no naming conventions or tagging strategy quickly becomes unsearchable. The organization layer — experiment groupings, run names, tags — is as important as the infrastructure that stores the data.

cards.title: Integrating Tracking Into the ML Pipeline
cards.teaser: Experiment tracking is only valuable if it runs on every training execution — not just when a data scientist remembers to add log calls. The production pattern is tracking-in-the-platform: tracking calls embedded in the training framework, triggered automatically by the pipeline orchestrator.

runs.text: Ad hoc tracking — adding
mlflow.log_metric()
calls manually when they seem important — produces an incomplete record with coverage gaps. The production pattern is to make tracking
mandatory and automatic

items.text: : define a base class or decorator that initializes a tracking run, logs the complete config object at start, and logs metrics via callbacks. All training scripts inherit from or use this class. Tracking is structural, not optional.

: ML pipeline orchestrators (Kubeflow Pipelines, Metaflow, ZenML, Prefect) support tracking integration at the task level. When a training task is defined as a pipeline component, tracking initialization and finalization are part of the component contract.
at pipeline startup to capture the framework-level logs automatically, then add explicit
calls for business-relevant metrics that the framework does not capture.
: training jobs that complete without a corresponding tracking run entry are flagged as pipeline failures. This enforces tracking completeness at the infrastructure level, not the honor system.

runs.text: The integration also determines what happens at the
end

of a successful run: automatic model registration, promotion to Staging if metrics exceed a threshold, and notification to the review queue. The tracking system becomes the control plane for the model lifecycle, not just a log storage layer.

Tracking only works as infrastructure if it runs on every training job automatically, not just when someone remembers to add log calls. Embed tracking into your base training framework or pipeline components so it is structural — and fail the pipeline if a run completes without a tracking record.
